author: DarkWebInformer
text: 🚨 Apache Roller is being actively exploited through a critical unauthenticated deserialization flaw; CVE-2026-129448 PoC: https://t.co/njSwpgIBGR The vulnerability affects Roller’s XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authenticating the requester. An unauthenticated remote attacker can abuse this behavior to execute arbitrary code. Apache Roller | Unauthenticated RCE: • CVSS: 9.8 Critical • Attack: Remote, unauthenticated • Affected: Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 • Fixed: Upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later • Impact: Arbitrary code execution • Status: Actively exploited in the wild The issue is the same underlying vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which previously listed a much narrower affected-version range. Apache recommends upgrading immediately or disabling extension types and removing the vulnerable XML-RPC servlet mapping if an upgrade cannot be performed yet.

author: DailyDarkWeb
text: 🚨 NEW ANALYSIS OF EXPLOITED CITRIX NETSCALER ZERO-DAY CVE-2026-88771 A new public root-cause analysis (published Nov 18) breaks down CVE-2026-88771, the critical NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaw Citrix disclosed on Sep 27, 2026. How the attack works, per the analysis: • A failed, unauthenticated management login writes attacker-controlled text to the appliance log • A root-owned maintenance script later reads that log text and passes it to a shell command • Result: unauthenticated remote code execution as root Key facts (Citrix bulletin CTX697096): • CVSS v4.0: 9.5 (critical) • Affected: all customer-managed NetScaler ADC and Gateway deployments, default config, no extra feature needed • Versions: 14.1 before 14.1-73.37, 13.1 before 13.1-64.23, 14.1-FIPS before 14.1-73.37 FIPS, 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP before 13.1-37.279 • Fixed: 14.1-73.37+, 13.1-64.23+, 14.1-73.37 FIPS+, 13.1-37.279+ (FIPS/NDcPP) • Exploitation: confirmed in the wild; CISA added it to the KEV catalog on Sep 27, 2026. The analysis says attackers reportedly used it as a zero-day for at least two weeks before disclosure ⚠️ Analyst Note: This is not a new flaw, and patches have been out since late September. The new write-up helps defenders understand the bug, and it also helps attackers. Patching does not remove web shells or rogue accounts already planted, so exposed appliances that ran a vulnerable build should be treated as potential incident-response cases: preserve logs, rotate credentials and hunt for compromise. https://t.co/7OBKGiWcOh #DDW #Citrix #NetScaler #CVE202688771 #ZeroDay #RCE #ThreatIntelligence #CyberSecurity

author: Ghost_Jacker
text: Over the past roughly 24 hours, major cybersecurity incidents have primarily centered on supply chain attacks, phishing campaigns exploiting service outages, and actively exploited vulnerabilities despite available patches. Microsoft-related incidents remain in focus, though no new large-scale system intrusions or massive data breaches have been confirmed. 1. Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI Package Compromised with Credential-Stealing Malware On November 17, attackers published malicious versions (1.26.1 and 1.26.2) of Microsoft’s official agent-framework package to PyPI, which remained live for approximately 45 minutes before being quarantined. Using a .pth startup hook, the malware executed automatically upon Python startup (even without importing the package), stealing cloud and developer credentials—including Azure, GitHub Actions, CI/CD secrets, environment variables, and credential files—and exfiltrating them to a webhook. The package sees roughly 190,000 monthly downloads; Microsoft has confirmed the incident and is investigating. * Scope of Impact: Developer workstations, CI/CD pipelines, and containers that installed the two malicious versions (recommended to be treated as compromised, with immediate credential rotation). * Sources: SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, CSO Online, GitHub Advisory, etc. (reported November 18, 2026). 2. Attackers Exploit Microsoft 365 Outage to Launch High-Volume Credential Phishing Following the November 12–13 global outage affecting Microsoft 365, Outlook, and Exchange Online (officially attributed to a latent software bug combined with network capacity issues, rather than a cyberattack), threat actors sent spoofed Microsoft service health notification emails. Citing the real incident ID EX1550543, the emails falsely claimed that quarantined messages would be deleted within 24 hours, luring victims to click a "Restore Messages" link. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses the campaign as credential phishing, with no confirmed credential theft or malware payloads observed yet. * Scope of Impact: Multiple U.S. sectors (with some reports extending to Europe and Asia), involving high email volumes. * Sources: Computerworld, Cybernews, Microsoft Threat Intelligence, GBHackers (November 16–18). 3. Outlook Zero-Day CVE-2026-124194 Remains Actively Exploited as Patch Deadline Nears Microsoft patched this moderate-severity (CVSS 6.5) Outlook spoofing vulnerability during its November 10 Patch Tuesday release. When an attacker tricks a user into opening a specially crafted message file, Outlook connects to an attacker-controlled server without displaying an external content warning, leaking NTLMv2 hashes (which can be used for impersonation or relay attacks). CISA has added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, mandating federal agencies to patch by November 24. It is the only confirmed actively exploited flaw among the more than 1,000 vulnerabilities patched this month. * Scope of Impact: Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021 / 2024. * Sources: SecurityWeek, The Hacker News, Malwarebytes, CISA KEV (ongoing coverage through mid-November). 4. Optimizely Supply Chain Attack Injects Malware into 178 Major Websites On November 16, attackers exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects, affecting at least 178 organizational websites (including Zoom, HSBC, CNN, BBC, Salesforce, and IKEA). The malware is capable of payment card skimming, cryptocurrency wallet address swapping, cookie and screenshot theft, and delivering an exploit kit targeting iOS devices. Optimizely has patched the vulnerability and removed the malicious code. * Scope of Impact: Visitors to the affected websites across finance, media, technology, and other sectors. * Sources: SecurityWeek, TechTarget, Krebs on Security, CSO Online (November 17–18).

author: ptdbugs
text: A PoC/exploit has been discovered for vulnerability CVE-2026-129448 PT ID: PT-2026-148853 Read on dbugs: https://t.co/OTPzegjeBt Vendor: Apache Software Foundation Product: Apache Roller Description: Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester. This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. This issue is being actively exploited. Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled. Users who cannot upgrade right away should set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and restart Roller. Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting. Link: https://t.co/p3THcwk1Bv

text: CISA has confirmed active exploitation of a vulnerability in LiteLLM, an AI gateway used to manage access to language models. author: wealthcompoun
text: AI-driven cyberattacks evolve as autonomous systems begin exploiting vulnerabilities Google has identified what it described as the first observed cyberattack in which an AI-powered system independently discovered and exploited software vulnerabilities without human intervention, highlighting the growing threat of autonomous cyber operations. A report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant warns that threat actors are moving beyond using AI as an assistant towards deploying multi-agent systems capable of planning and executing multiple stages of cyber intrusions. AI-enabled autonomous attacks: Systems can automate reconnaissance, identify software weaknesses, generate malicious code and modify tactics based on execution feedback. Google discovered an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent, connected to advanced locally hosted LLMs. The framework examined software updates, compared code before and after security patches, identified vulnerabilities and developed exploits. Scripts on the server supported post-intrusion activities such as network reconnaissance, brute-force attempts and webshell installation. The operator appeared to target French websites associated with media, entertainment and education. Growing ecosystem of offensive AI frameworks: Google identified increasing adoption of open-source multi-agent platforms, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI and HexStrike AI. CAIRN uses an Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (OODA) approach to coordinate autonomous actions. Google observed CAIRN-related intrusion activity targeting organisations, including those in the US aerospace sector. A threat actor using a customised PentAGI-based framework conducted reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning across Asian organisations between late August and early October 2026. Tools such as ZeroHollow and Agent Zero are also being used for exploit development, LLM routing, code execution and dynamic tool generation. Exploitation timelines are shrinking: AI is accelerating differential patch analysis, in which attackers compare software versions before and after security patches to identify vulnerabilities before organisations patch their systems. Vulnerability disclosures and exploitation nearly doubled between January and August 2026, according to the report. Average monthly zero-day exploits rose from eight in 2025 to 11 in 2026, reaching 22 in August. In the August PaperCut vulnerability incidents, researchers developed working exploits within a day of disclosure. A subsequent campaign involved AI-assisted exploit development and attacks against hundreds of organisations, with one attacker reportedly reaching domain administrator privileges within minutes. Other emerging threats: Espionage and influence operations: Groups linked to Russia, China and Iran are using LLMs for research, social engineering, data analysis and synthetic content generation. LLMJacking: Criminals steal cloud credentials to access AI models and computing resources, generating fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day and losses of up to $1 million in some investigations. Supply-chain attacks: Attempts to manipulate autonomous coding assistant configurations could introduce backdoors during local execution. AI-generated exploits are not always successful, but the lower barrier to developing malicious code is increasing the burden on security teams to verify and respond to attacks. Takeaway: AI is compressing cyberattack timelines, automating complex intrusion stages and lowering the technical barrier to sophisticated cybercrime. Faster patching, stronger credential security, monitoring of AI-agent activity and tighter controls over autonomous coding tools are becoming increasingly critical for organisations.

author: NedPeterson99
text: A ten-year-old NGINX bug, found by AI, with a working chain to root on your cloud host. F5 shipped emergency patches for 10 open-source NGINX CVEs on Wednesday. Two are critical 9.2 unauthenticated RCEs in the HTTP/2 code path, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, the latter present since 1.9.5 in 2015. Wiz, Rapid7, Xint and others found them independently, most with an AI assist; Xint's fully automated scan then found four more with no human guidance, including a Linux kernel flaw it chained with the NGINX bugs to escape the container and take root on AWS, Azure and GCP hosts. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept. F5 says it has seen no exploitation in the wild so far. The lesson for CISOs: NGINX fronts roughly a third of the web, and the gap between a vendor patch and a weaponized exploit is now days, not weeks. Inventory every NGINX instance, including the ones buried in ingress controllers and vendor appliances, upgrade to 1.31.9, and disable HTTP/2 where you cannot patch today. https://t.co/F7zQ51IRig #CloudSecurity #CNAPP #CyberSecurity

author: nisyron
text: PromptArmor released FrontierBreach yesterday. 34.9% of hidden-instruction attacks against enterprise AI agents succeeded across 21 models. Grok 4.5 hit 91.4%. The predictable take: "we need safer models." The real take: model safety was never the bottleneck. Hidden instructions embedded in third-party agent skills succeeded 45.5% of the time. Email connectors 33.9%. Document systems 31.5%. Even the "safest" model on the benchmark (Gemini 4 Argon at 4.3%) gets compromised the moment it reads a poisoned file or calls an untrusted skill. The attack surface is the tool chain, not the model. And the industry keeps treating prompt injection as a model-level vulnerability when it is fundamentally an architectural one. You cannot prompt-engineer your way out of an agent that reads emails, executes skills, and accesses files. The model is not the perimeter. The tool chain is. And right now, most organizations have no visibility into what their agents are actually doing across that chain. The FrontierBreach numbers are scary. But the real story is that we are deploying agents into enterprise environments without runtime controls, without tool-level audit trails, and without the ability to intervene mid-execution. That is not a model problem. That is a deployment problem.
